title: Can Dogs Eat Pumpkin? Seeds, Puree & Safety Guide
summary: Can dogs eat pumpkin? Learn which parts are safe, how to prep pumpkin seeds, why plain puree beats pie filling, and how much pumpkin to give your dog.

Fall brings pumpkins onto porches, into pies, and inevitably within reach of our dogs. Having worked extensively in pet nutrition research, I’ve encountered pumpkin often, particularly in discussions about dietary fiber and soothing[upset tummies](https://petcube.com/blog/is-your-dogs-stomach-making-noises/) naturally. But while a little plain pumpkin can be a useful addition to[a dog’s diet](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-vegetables/) , not everything inside your jack-o’-lantern belongs in their bowl.


**Content:**


1. Is Pumpkin Safe for Dogs? The Basics
2. Pumpkin Seeds: Raw, Roasted, Shelled & How to Prep Them Safely
3. Guts, Skin, Rind & Stem: Which Parts Are Safe?
4. Pumpkin Treats, Pie, Spice & Canned Puree
5. Conclusion


## Is Pumpkin Safe for Dogs? The Basics


Yes, dogs can eat pumpkin. Plain, cooked pumpkin is generally the safest choice, while 100% canned pumpkin puree is another convenient option. Raw pumpkin isn’t considered toxic, but it’s tougher to digest, so I prefer cooked pumpkin when feeding it deliberately.


Pumpkin is best known as a source of dietary fiber. However, it shouldn’t be treated as a cure-all for digestive problems.


Veterinary nutritionist[Dr. Valerie Parker](https://www.dvm360.com/view/veterinary-heroes-valerie-j-parker-dvm-dacvim-saim-nutrition-?ref=petcube.com) notes that common supplemental fiber sources include “psyllium husk, cellulose, or canned pumpkin.” Importantly, veterinary literature also points out that different fiber sources vary considerably in their fiber concentrations and effects.


In other words, pumpkin can be useful, but more isn’t necessarily better. Dogs also don’t need as much fiber as humans do, so while a little can be good and nutritious, too much fiber can interfere with how they absorb[nutrients](https://petcube.com/blog/vitamins-dog-needs-for-healthy-life/) or cause digestive issues.


On[Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/dogs/comments/gzn43v/help_has_anyone_ever_given_their_dog_pumpkin_to/?ref=petcube.com) , one pet parent wrote:


> “My friend is studying to become a veterinarian and she told me that giving my dog a little bit of pumpkin with his breakfast can help him poop more regularly and also increase his fiber intake as well as soothe his stomach and aid digestion.”


That’s also a good description of how I approach serving size: a little bit.


Start with a small amount rather than suddenly adding a large dose of fiber. Too much too quickly can cause gas,[bloating](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-bloating/) , cramping, or changes in bowel movements.


## Pumpkin Seeds: Raw, Roasted, Shelled & How to Prep Them Safely


Dogs can eat plain pumpkin seeds, but preparation matters. You can remove the shells where possible and offer seeds plain, without any kind of salt, oil, butter, sugar, or seasoning.


Roasted seeds can be given occasionally if they’re completely plain. For smaller dogs especially, crushing or grinding the seeds can also make them easier to eat.


Seeds are calorie-dense, though, and while a little probably won’t hurt, there’s no reason for seeds to be a major part of a dog’s diet.


## Guts, Skin, Rind & Stem: Which Parts Are Safe?


When carving pumpkins, keep the scraps away from your dog, as these aren’t safe for them.


The soft flesh is the part worth sharing. But I highly recommend removing the stringy guts, tough skin and rind, and the stem. These aren’t necessarily poisonous, but they’re difficult to digest, and large pieces can present a[choking](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-choking/) or[gastrointestinal obstruction](https://petcube.com/blog/swollen-dog-belly/) risk.


Cooked, mashed flesh is much easier on the digestive tract.


## Pumpkin Treats, Pie, Spice & Canned Puree


This is where “pumpkin” becomes a dangerously broad category.


Plain canned pumpkin puree? Fine. It’s not bad for dogs, but the benefits of a teaspoon or so may be slightly overstated in terms of how much fiber it actually contains.


Pumpkin pie filling, on the other hand, is not a good idea. Pie filling and other seasonal pumpkin products may contain large amounts of sugar, fat, spices, or sweeteners that dogs don’t need.


And if you’re using pumpkin because your dog already has ongoing[diarrhea](https://petcube.com/blog/diarrhea-in-dogs/) ,[constipation](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-constipation/) ,[vomiting](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-vomiting/) , or other digestive symptoms, pumpkin shouldn’t substitute for veterinary care. The[Petcube App](https://petcube.com/promo/atp-w2w/?ref=petcube.com) can help you stay connected to your pet and access veterinary support when something doesn’t look right.


## Conclusion


Pumpkin can absolutely be part of a[dog-friendly fall](https://petcube.com/blog/thanksgiving-foods-your-pet-can-eat/) , but keep it boring. Plain cooked pumpkin or pure pumpkin puree beats pie, spices, sugary treats, and jack-o’-lantern leftovers every time. Introduce it gradually, keep portions modest, and remember that pumpkin is simply one useful source of fiber, not a treatment for every upset stomach.
